anchor.note: English 'for' is the comparison anchor. The lesson teaches semantic relationships rather than one-to-one translations.

scope_note: Common words, case markers, particles, and constructions used for semantic territory that English often expresses with 'for'. Language entries are independent; no language inherits another language's rules.

rules.summary_en: English uses 'for' across several different relationships, including recipient, reason, duration, exchange, intended use, and destination-like expressions.
tips_en: Treat English 'for' as the question, not the answer.
Before translating, ask what relationship 'for' expresses in this sentence.

rules.summary_en: Path, route, or area moved through or along.
tips_en: Picture movement through the middle of something.
If the phrase answers 'through/by what route?', check por.

rules.summary_en: Cause, reason, or motivation.
tips_en: Look backward for what caused the action.
If 'because of' fits naturally, check por.

rules.summary_en: The expression por qué asks for a reason.
tips_en: Treat por qué as a whole expression.
If the answer gives a reason, por qué is the question form.

rules.summary_en: Por eso links a prior reason to its consequence.
tips_en: Por eso points backward to what was just explained.
Think 'because of that' rather than translating por alone.

rules.summary_en: Means, method, route, channel, or medium.
tips_en: Ask how or by what channel something happened.
Method, route, mail, and similar channel meanings often use por.

rules.summary_en: Exchange, price, replacement, or substitution.
tips_en: Think one thing in exchange for another.
Prices and substitutions commonly live on the por side.

rules.summary_en: Distributive patterns such as uno por uno.
tips_en: Look for a repeated unit: one by one, person by person.
A per-unit pattern is a good clue for por.

rules.summary_en: Intended purpose or goal, especially para + infinitive.
tips_en: Look forward to what the action is trying to accomplish.
If 'in order to' fits, check para.

rules.summary_en: Destination, endpoint, or goal.
tips_en: Picture an arrow pointing toward an endpoint.
An intended destination usually points to para.

rules.summary_en: Intended recipient or beneficiary.
tips_en: Ask who the thing is intended for.
Recipient or beneficiary usually points to para.

rules.summary_en: Deadline or target time.
tips_en: Think of the time as a target you are aiming toward.
A due date usually lives on the para side.

rules.summary_en: Cause, motive, or reason in many common uses.
tips_en: Look backward for the reason something happened.
Portuguese por overlaps Spanish por here, but do not assume every rule is shared.

rules.summary_en: Path, route, or movement through a place.
tips_en: Think movement through or around a place.
Route meanings commonly point to por.

rules.summary_en: Means, medium, or channel.
tips_en: Ask how something was sent, communicated, or accomplished.
A channel or method often points to por.

rules.summary_en: Exchange, substitution, price, or per-unit relationship.
tips_en: Look for exchange or per-unit meaning.
Prices and replacement relationships commonly use por.

rules.summary_en: Intention, purpose, objective, or intended use.
tips_en: Ask what the action or object is intended to accomplish.
Intended use commonly points to para.

rules.summary_en: Direction or destination.
tips_en: Picture an endpoint being aimed at.
Destination is a strong para clue.

rules.summary_en: Recipient or beneficiary.
tips_en: Ask who receives or benefits from it.
An intended recipient is a strong para clue.

rules.summary_en: Target time or deadline in common constructions.
tips_en: Think target date, not elapsed duration.
When time is an endpoint, check para.

rules.summary_en: Cause or motive in the central per/per a contrast.
tips_en: Look backward for the reason or cause.
Catalan usage is construction- and variety-sensitive, so learn the phrase, not only the label.

rules.summary_en: Path, means, and several other relationships also use per.
tips_en: Do not reduce Catalan to only cause versus purpose.
Check the specific construction for route and means uses.

rules.summary_en: Purpose or intended use in the constructions that take per a.
tips_en: Look forward to the intended purpose.
Before an infinitive and in some varieties, the surface choice is more nuanced, so follow the reviewed construction record.

rules.summary_en: Destination, intended recipient, or beneficiary in many uses.
tips_en: Ask what or whom the action is directed toward.
An intended endpoint or recipient often points toward per a.

languages.notes: Catalan per/per a usage varies by construction and normative/dialect context; these are lesson-family candidate rules, not a claim of a universal binary.

rules.summary_en: Path or movement through an area.
tips_en: Think route through a place.
Path meanings commonly point to por.

rules.summary_en: Cause or motive.
tips_en: Look backward for the cause.
Because-of meanings often use por.

rules.summary_en: Por can also express purpose/finality in Galician.
tips_en: This is where importing the Spanish split can mislead you.
Galician por can carry purpose in constructions where Spanish would push you toward para.

rules.summary_en: Price, means, substitution, or per-unit relationships.
tips_en: Prices, transmission, replacement, and per-unit patterns often use por.
Use the construction rather than an English gloss to decide.

rules.summary_en: Purpose, intended use, or suitability.
tips_en: Ask what something is intended to do or be used for.
Purpose is common with para but is not exclusive to para in Galician.

rules.summary_en: Direction or destination.
tips_en: Picture movement toward an endpoint.
Direction and destination commonly use para.

rules.summary_en: Target or relevant time in common uses.
tips_en: Think of the time as a target point.
Contrast this with por when the meaning is elapsed duration.

rules.summary_en: Recipient or intended beneficiary.
tips_en: Ask who receives or is targeted by the action.
Recipient meanings commonly use para.

languages.notes: Galician has meaningful por/para overlap; it must never inherit the Spanish decision boundary.

rules.summary_en: Direction or destination in many common expressions.
tips_en: Think movement or orientation toward an endpoint.
Greek για itself covers several English-for relationships, so context still matters.

rules.summary_en: Cause or reason in some constructions.
tips_en: Ask whether the phrase explains why something happened.
Greek does not need a Spanish-style word switch for every cause/purpose contrast.

rules.summary_en: Purpose, intended use, recipient, or suitability in many noun-phrase constructions.
tips_en: Ask what or whom something is intended for.
With an explicit purpose clause, Greek often uses για να instead.

rules.summary_en: Introduces an explicit purpose clause, roughly 'in order to'.
tips_en: If English can naturally say 'in order to', look for για να.
Treat για να as a construction, not as a word-for-word translation puzzle.

rules.summary_en: Explicit cause or reason, often corresponding to 'because of'.
tips_en: Use the cause relationship as your clue.
Λόγω is a more explicit causal option than generic για.

rules.summary_en: Support or advocacy: being 'for' a person, proposal, or side.
tips_en: Think 'in favor of' rather than recipient-for.
Support/advocacy is a separate relationship from purpose.

languages.notes: Greek qualifies because English 'for' maps across multiple Greek forms/constructions; Greek is not modeled as a two-word por/para analogue.
